docs.title: Company Party — Domain Model
docs.text: Status: draft for review. Owner: Solution Architecture. Date: 2026-11-03.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A Company is an organisation represented as a Party. It has a stable Party identifier and identity details describing the organisation. Depending on the jurisdiction and business context, it may be a registered legal entity or another recognised organisational form.

A Company record describes which organisation this is. It does not, by itself, describe the organisation's role in a matter, its owners or controllers, an individual's authority to act for it, or the outcome of a company verification or compliance check. Those facts belong to separately modelled relationships or processes.

docs.title: Relationship to Party
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Party {
        partyId
        type
        displayName
        status
        createdAt
        updatedAt
    }
    class Company {
        legalName
        tradingNames
        legalForm
        registrationIdentifiers
        jurisdiction
        registeredAddress
        contactMethods
    }
    class GroupMembership {
        role
        validFrom
        validTo
    }
    class Participation {
        contextId
        role
    }
    class CompanyRelationship {
        relationshipType
        validFrom
        validTo
    }
    Party <|-- Company
    Company "0..*" -- "0..*" GroupMembership : member of
    Company "0..*" -- "0..*" Participation : participates in
    Company "0..*" -- "0..*" CompanyRelationship : related to Parties

This is a conceptual model. Company may be implemented as a Party subtype or as type-specific details associated with a Party record. There must be one stable Party identity either way.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Requiredness Description partyId Required Stable identifier for this organization as a Party. Generated by the Party service; not derived from its name or registration number. type Required Always company. It cannot be changed in place to individual or group. displayName Required Human-readable name used in lists and references. May use the legal name or an appropriate trading name. legalName Conditional Name under which the organization is legally constituted or registered, where applicable. tradingNames Optional, repeatable Current or former business names, with source and effective dates where known. A trading name is not a separate Company unless independently represented as one. legalForm Optional, jurisdiction-dependent Organizational or legal form, using a defined code set where a consuming process requires it. registrationIdentifiers Optional, repeatable and sensitive Registration number or other official identifier, including identifier type, issuing jurisdiction/authority, and relevant dates. Values are not assumed globally unique. jurisdiction Conditional Country or jurisdiction of formation or registration, represented with the agreed code standard. Do not infer this from an address. registeredAddress Optional, purpose-dependent Registered office or official address, where applicable, with effective dates and source where required. businessAddresses Optional, repeatable Operating or correspondence addresses, distinguished by purpose and effective dates. Do not assume an address is a registered office. contactMethods Optional, repeatable Organization contact methods, with type, value, preferred indicator, and verification state where applicable. taxIdentifiers Optional, repeatable and highly sensitive Tax identifiers, each scoped by type and issuing jurisdiction. Collect and expose only for an approved purpose. status Required Party-record status, such as active or inactive. This is distinct from legal standing, dissolution, or insolvency status. createdAt, updatedAt Required Record creation and most recent update timestamps.

Fields marked conditional or optional are not universally required to create a Company. A consuming process defines the attributes it needs and validates them before that process proceeds. Avoid storing empty placeholders or collecting identifiers “just in case.”

docs.title: Group membership
docs.text: A Company can be a member of zero or more groups. Membership is a separate, effective-dated relationship and may include a group-specific role, such as corporate purchaser or subsidiary. Group membership alone does not establish ownership, control, or legal authority.

docs.title: Matter or process participation
docs.text: A Company can participate in zero or more matters or processes. The participation relationship carries the context-specific role, such as seller, borrower, or counterparty. A Company's role in one matter must not be copied onto its Party identity or assumed in another matter.

docs.title: Relationships to individuals and other companies
docs.text:
Officers, directors, agents, owners, beneficial owners, parent companies, and subsidiaries should be represented as explicit, typed relationships when required. Such relationships may have effective dates, source, and verification evidence. They must not be inferred solely from shared names, addresses, group membership, or a free-text note.

The relationship model must distinguish a person's role or authority to act from the person's own identity. Rules for ownership thresholds, control, and evidence are defined by the consuming business process or jurisdiction-specific policy.

docs.title: Verification and compliance
docs.text: Company verification results, screening findings, decisions, and evidence are owned by the relevant process. They reference the Company Party but are not intrinsic identity attributes. A verification outcome must not silently overwrite the organization's identity details or legal status.

docs.title: Constraints and behavior
docs.text:
• Each Company is one Party with a stable identifier and type company.
  • Names and addresses are descriptive attributes, not unique keys. Organizations may share similar names, change legal or trading names, or use different scripts.
  • Registration identifiers are interpreted in the context of their type and issuing jurisdiction; they are not assumed globally unique.
  • A Company may be represented even when it has no registration identifier, if its organizational form or the consuming process permits it.
  • Legal form, jurisdiction, legal standing, and Party-record status are distinct concepts and must not be conflated.
  • Identity corrections and changes to official details are authorized and auditable; historical process records remain interpretable.
  • Address and contact changes do not rewrite previously recorded process snapshots or evidence.
  • Inactivation is reversible only through an authorized action and must be audited.
  • Sensitive registration and tax identifiers are returned only to callers with the appropriate authorization.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
partyId: party_01JEXAMPLE
type: company
displayName: "Example Holdings Limited"
status: active
company:
  legalName: "Example Holdings Limited"
  tradingNames: []
  legalForm: null
  jurisdiction: null
  registrationIdentifiers: []
  registeredAddress: null
  businessAddresses: []
  contactMethods: []
  taxIdentifiers: []

The example is illustrative, not an API contract. Optional organizational information is omitted unless a legitimate use case requires it.

docs.title: Open decisions
docs.text:
1. Which organizational forms count as a Company Party, including partnerships, trusts, charities, public bodies, and unincorporated associations?
  2. Which identifier types and jurisdiction code standards are in scope for the first consumers?
  3. Should names and registered details retain full field-level history, or are attributed audit events and process-specific snapshots sufficient?
  4. Which sources are authoritative for legal name, registration status, addresses, officers, and ownership relationships?
  5. Which company relationships are needed in the MVP, and which systems own their validation and evidence?
  6. What access controls, masking, retention, and anonymisation rules apply to registration and tax identifiers?
  7. Should Party maintain legal standing (for example, dissolved or in liquidation), or should that be a separately sourced and time-stamped status record?

docs.title: Relationship to CDD
docs.text: The current CDD/KYC model uses Subject for a person or company. If Company Party becomes the canonical organization identity record, CDD should reference its Party identifier and keep journey-specific requirements, evidence, findings, and decisions on the CDD journey. Company verification and ownership/control evidence should be linked to the relevant journey and source, not treated as timeless identity facts. The integration contract must define whether CDD stores a reference only or also a minimal, time-stamped snapshot needed to interpret historical decisions.

docs.title: Individual Party — Domain Model
docs.text: Status: draft for review. Owner: Solution Architecture. Date: 2026-11-03.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An Individual is a natural person represented as a Party. The Individual has a stable Party identifier and identity details that describe the person. The same Individual may participate in multiple matters and may be a member of multiple groups.

An Individual record describes who the person is. It does not, by itself, describe the person's role in a matter, their relationship to a company or group, their authority to act, or the outcome of an identity or compliance check. Those facts belong to separately modeled relationships or processes.

docs.title: Relationship to Party
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class Party {
        partyId
        type
        displayName
        status
        createdAt
        updatedAt
    }
    class Individual {
        givenNames
        familyName
        dateOfBirth
        nationality
        contactMethods
        addresses
        identifiers
    }
    class GroupMembership {
        role
        validFrom
        validTo
    }
    class Participation {
        contextId
        role
    }
    Party <|-- Individual
    Individual "0..*" -- "0..*" GroupMembership : member of
    Individual "0..*" -- "0..*" Participation : participates in

This is a conceptual model. Individual may be implemented as a Party subtype or as type-specific details associated with a Party record. There must be one stable Party identity either way.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Requiredness Description partyId Required Stable identifier for this person as a Party. Generated by the Party service; not derived from a name or government identifier. type Required Always individual. It cannot be changed in place to company or group. displayName Required Human-readable name used in lists and references. May be derived from the person's name, but can preserve an appropriate display form. givenNames Conditional One or more given names, when known and relevant. familyName Conditional Family name, when applicable. The model must not require a family name for a person whose naming convention does not use one. dateOfBirth Optional, purpose-dependent Date of birth. Collect and expose only when required by an approved process. nationalities Optional, repeatable Zero or more nationalities, represented with country codes and, where needed, effective dates or source. Nationality is not the same as country of residence or place of birth. contactMethods Optional, repeatable Email, telephone, or other permitted contact method, with type, value, preferred indicator, and verification state where applicable. addresses Optional, repeatable Structured address with purpose, country code, and effective dates where required. A person's address is not assumed to be their permanent residence. identifiers Optional, repeatable and sensitive External identity references, each with identifier type, value, issuing country/authority, and relevant validity dates. Apply field-level access controls and masking. status Required Lifecycle status, such as active or inactive. Inactivation preserves historical references and does not mean the person is deceased. createdAt, updatedAt Required Record creation and most recent update timestamps.

Fields marked conditional or optional are not universally required to create an Individual. A consuming process defines which attributes it needs and validates them before that process proceeds. Avoid storing empty placeholders or collecting sensitive attributes “just in case.”

docs.title: Group membership
docs.text: An Individual can be a member of zero or more groups. Membership is a separate, effective-dated relationship and may include a group-specific role, such as beneficiary or joint purchaser. Ending membership closes the relationship; it does not delete the Individual or change the person's identity.

docs.title: Matter or process participation
docs.text: An Individual can participate in zero or more matters or processes. The participation relationship carries the context-specific role, such as purchaser, director, or counterparty. A person's role in one matter must not be copied onto their Party identity or assumed in another matter.

docs.title: Verification and consent
docs.text: Verification results, screening findings, decisions, and consent evidence are owned by the relevant process. They reference the Individual Party but are not intrinsic identity attributes. A verification outcome must not silently overwrite the person's identity details.

docs.title: Constraints and behavior
docs.text:
• Each Individual is one Party with a stable identifier and type individual.
  • Names are descriptive attributes, not unique keys. Two people may share a name, and one person may have multiple or changed name forms.
  • External identifiers are not assumed globally unique. Their meaning is scoped by identifier type and issuing jurisdiction or authority.
  • A person can exist without a date of birth, nationality, address, or contact method unless a consuming process requires a particular field.
  • Name and identity corrections update the Party through an authorized, auditable change; historical process records must remain interpretable.
  • Contact and address changes do not rewrite previously recorded process snapshots or evidence.
  • The model must support a mononym or other naming convention without inventing a given name or family name.
  • Inactivation is reversible only through an authorized action and must be audited.
  • Sensitive fields are returned only to callers with the appropriate authorization.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
partyId: party_01JEXAMPLE
type: individual
displayName: "Alex Morgan"
status: active
individual:
  givenNames:
    - Alex
  familyName: Morgan
  dateOfBirth: null
  nationalities: []
  contactMethods:
    - type: email
      value: alex@example.invalid
      preferred: true
      verificationStatus: unverified
  addresses: []
  identifiers: []

The example is illustrative, not an API contract. Optional personal information is omitted unless a legitimate use case requires it.

docs.title: Open decisions
docs.text:
1. Which name components and alternate-name forms must be supported for the initial consumers?
  2. Which country-code standard and address format should the service standardize on?
  3. Which identifier types can be stored, who can read them, and what masking is required?
  4. Should contact verification state be maintained by Party or by the process that collected and verified the contact method?
  5. What are the approved retention and erasure/anonymisation rules for individual identity attributes?
  6. Should Party maintain current details only, or full field-level history in addition to the audit log and process-specific snapshots?

docs.title: Relationship to CDD
docs.text: The current CDD/KYC model uses Subject for a person or company. If Individual Party becomes the canonical identity record, CDD should reference its Party identifier and keep journey-specific requirements, evidence, findings, and decisions on the CDD journey. The integration contract must define whether CDD stores a reference only or also a minimal, time-stamped snapshot needed to interpret historical decisions.

docs.title: Party — Product Requirements Document
docs.text: Status: draft for review. Owner: Solution Architecture. Date: 2026-11-03.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Party is a reusable, authoritative record for a person, a company, or a group made up of people and/or companies. Other business processes can refer to a Party rather than creating their own disconnected copy of a client, counterparty, or related entity.

A group is itself a Party. It represents a business-relevant collection of people and/or companies, such as joint purchasers, a family, a corporate group, or a group of beneficiaries. Membership and each member's role are recorded explicitly.

The product must distinguish the identity of a Party from its participation in a matter or process. A Party may be reused in many contexts; its context-specific role belongs to the relationship or process, not to the Party's identity.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Business processes need to record individuals, companies, and arrangements involving more than one of either. If each process models these independently, the same person or company can be duplicated, group membership is difficult to represent, and downstream processes cannot reliably tell who a record represents.

The existing CDD/KYC domain model describes a Subject as a person or company. It does not yet define a reusable Party concept or a group that can be assessed as one participant while retaining its constituent members.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Represent an individual, a company, or a group of individuals and/or companies consistently.
  • Make a Party reusable across matters and business processes.
  • Preserve the identity and details of group members while allowing the group itself to be referenced as a participant.
  • Record membership, roles, and changes with clear attribution and history.
  • Protect personal and commercially sensitive information through access control, minimisation, and auditability.
  • Give downstream systems a stable identifier and a clear way to determine the Party type and its members.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Performing identity verification, AML screening, or making compliance decisions.
  • Replacing matter, customer, CRM, or case-management systems.
  • Defining the legal meaning or authority of a group; processes remain responsible for validating that a group can act in a particular capacity.
  • Automatically merging records based only on approximate name matches.
  • Modeling arbitrary nested groups in the MVP. Whether a group can contain another group remains an open question.

docs.title: Users and responsibilities
docs.text: User Need Case handler / adviser Find or create the right person, company, or group and record its role in a matter. Operations Correct Party details and membership while preserving an audit history. Compliance reviewer Understand who was assessed, including the constituents of a group. Integrating systems Create or reference Parties reliably without duplicating identity data. Administrator / privacy officer Control access to sensitive data and support retention and correction obligations.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
Concept Meaning Party A stable, reusable business identity. Every Party has exactly one type: individual, company, or group. Individual A natural person represented as a Party; see individual model Company A legally or commercially recognized organization represented as a Party; see company model Group A Party composed of one or more member Parties. In the MVP, its members are individuals and/or companies. Membership A time-aware relationship between a group Party and a member Party, optionally describing the member's role in that group. Participation A relationship between a Party and a matter or process. It carries context-specific roles, such as purchaser or director, without changing the Party's identity. 
erDiagram
    PARTY ||--o| INDIVIDUAL_DETAILS : "has"
    PARTY ||--o| COMPANY_DETAILS : "has"
    PARTY ||--o{ GROUP_MEMBERSHIP : "has members"
    PARTY ||--o{ GROUP_MEMBERSHIP : "is a member"
    PARTY ||--o{ PARTICIPATION : "takes part in"

    PARTY {
        string id PK
        string type "individual | company | group"
        string display_name
        string status
        datetime created_at
        datetime updated_at
    }
    INDIVIDUAL_DETAILS {
        string party_id PK
        string given_names
        string family_name
        date date_of_birth
    }
    COMPANY_DETAILS {
        string party_id PK
        string legal_name
        string registration_number
        string registration_country
    }
    GROUP_MEMBERSHIP {
        string group_party_id FK
        string member_party_id FK
        string role
        date valid_from
        date valid_to
    }
    PARTICIPATION {
        string party_id FK
        string context_id
        string role
    }

The diagram is conceptual. The implementation may store subtype details differently, provided the Party type, membership, and identity boundaries remain explicit.

docs.title: Create or find a Party
docs.text:
1. A user or integrating system searches for an existing Party using available identifiers and descriptive details.
  2. Potential matches are shown with enough information to distinguish them, subject to the user's access permissions.
  3. The caller either selects an existing Party or creates a new Party of the correct type.
  4. The system assigns a stable Party identifier and records the creation event.

An uncertain match must be presented for review; the system must not silently merge records.

docs.title: Create a group Party
docs.text:
1. The user creates a Party with type group and a meaningful display name.
  2. The user adds one or more existing or newly created individual/company Parties as members.
  3. The user may record each member's group-specific role and membership dates.
  4. The resulting group Party can be referenced in a matter or process, while its members remain independently addressable.

docs.title: Update Party or membership details
docs.text:
1. An authorized user changes Party details or group membership.
  2. The system records who made the change, when it happened, and the fields or membership affected.
  3. Historical participation and decisions remain interpretable against the Party details and membership that applied at the relevant time.

docs.title: Functional requirements
docs.text: Priority: Must (required for MVP), Should (important but deferrable), Could (future enhancement).

docs.title: Identity and lifecycle
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement PRT-1 Must Every Party has a stable, unique identifier and exactly one type: individual, company, or group. PRT-2 Must A Party can be created, retrieved, searched, and updated by authorized users or systems. PRT-3 Must An individual Party supports a display name and structured person details; a company Party supports a legal name and available registration details. PRT-4 Must A group Party has a display name and at least one member before it is used in a business process. PRT-5 Must A group can contain both individual and company Parties. The same member may belong to more than one group. PRT-6 Must A Party used by a matter or process is referenced by its stable identifier; context-specific roles are recorded on the participation, not as intrinsic Party attributes. PRT-7 Must Party type cannot be changed in place. Correcting a wrongly typed record requires a controlled replacement or correction process that preserves references and history. PRT-8 Must A Party can be marked inactive or archived without deleting its historical references. PRT-9 Should Search supports identifiers and names, with type and status filters. PRT-10 Should Search can surface likely duplicates but does not automatically merge them.

docs.title: Group membership
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement GRP-1 Must Each membership links one group Party to one individual or company Party. GRP-2 Must Membership can include an optional role and effective start/end dates. GRP-3 Must Membership changes are auditable; ending a membership does not erase its history. GRP-4 Must A group cannot be its own member, and duplicate active membership links are rejected. GRP-5 Must A group cannot be used in a process if it has no active members; the user receives a clear validation error. GRP-6 Should The system can show the current and historical members of a group, including membership dates and roles. GRP-7 Could Support nested groups, subject to agreed rules for cycle prevention, effective membership, and whether nested members count as direct or indirect members.

docs.title: Access, privacy, and audit
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement SEC-1 Must Store only details needed for an approved business purpose; protect sensitive personal and company information in storage and transit. SEC-2 Must Access to and changes of sensitive Party data are authorized and auditable. SEC-3 Must Every create, update, membership change, archive, and merge/correction action records actor, time, and affected Party. SEC-4 Must Deactivation or correction does not silently alter historical matter or process records. SEC-5 Must Retention, correction, and anonymisation follow the applicable data-protection and records-retention policy. SEC-6 Should Access can be scoped by organization and business role, with sensitive fields restricted where required.

docs.title: Integration
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement INT-1 Must Integrating systems can create a Party or reference an existing Party by stable identifier. INT-2 Must A Party response identifies its type and provides the appropriate identity details; a group response identifies its members and membership roles/dates. INT-3 Must Invalid Party types, malformed identity details, invalid group membership, and unauthorized access return explicit errors rather than success-shaped defaults. INT-4 Should Create requests support an idempotency key so retries do not create duplicate Parties. INT-5 Should The Party service exposes enough information for downstream processes to identify whether a Party is an individual, company, or group and to resolve its members.

docs.title: Data principles
docs.text:
• Identity and process participation are separate: being a purchaser on one matter does not make someone a purchaser on every matter.
  • A group and its members are distinct Parties. Creating or updating the group does not overwrite the identity record of a member.
  • Membership is a relationship with a history, not a copied list of names.
  • Names are useful for display and search but are not reliable unique identifiers.
  • Do not infer legal authority, beneficial ownership, or control solely from group membership or a free-text role.
  • Store optional identity attributes only when justified by a consuming process.

docs.title: Success measures
docs.text: Measure Target Parties created with an explicit type 100% Group Parties used in a process with at least one active member 100% Party and membership changes with an attributable audit event 100% Duplicate Party creation caused by retried requests with idempotency enabled 0 Historical process records changed by Party updates 0 Unreviewed ambiguous match automatically merged 0

docs.title: MVP scope
docs.text:
The MVP includes:

  • Individual, company, and group Party types.
  • Creation, retrieval, update, search, and inactive/archive status.
  • Groups containing one or more individual and/or company Parties.
  • Optional member roles and effective membership dates.
  • Stable identifiers, validation, authorization, and auditable changes.
  • Downstream reference to a Party without copying its identity as a new record.

The MVP does not include nested groups, automatic record merging, legal ownership inference, or compliance decisioning.

docs.title: Dependencies and open questions
docs.text:
1. CDD alignment: Should Party become the canonical identity model replacing the current Subject (person/company), or should CDD retain a separate Subject that references Party? The domain contract must be agreed before integration.
  2. Nested groups: Can a group contain another group, or are groups limited to direct individual/company members? The MVP assumes direct members only.
  3. Group meaning: Are groups only a convenient way to represent joint parties, or must the model distinguish legal entities, households, beneficial ownership groups, and other group kinds?
  4. Group participation: When a group is used in a process, must every member automatically participate, or does the caller select the relevant members?
  5. Membership validation: Which membership roles and evidence are required for specific processes, and who is responsible for validating authority?
  6. Ownership and tenancy: Is Party shared globally, or scoped to an organization with controlled cross-organization reuse?
  7. Matching and merge: Which identifiers are authoritative for matching people and companies, and who can approve a merge or identity correction?
  8. Data policy: What are the approved retention periods, lawful basis, and anonymisation requirements for each Party type and process?

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• A user can create an individual Party, a company Party, and a group Party.
  • A group can include at least one individual and one company at the same time.
  • A group is addressable as one Party and its members are individually addressable.
  • Group membership can be added, ended, and inspected historically without deleting its audit history.
  • A downstream matter can reference a Party and assign a matter-specific role without changing the Party's identity or role in another matter.
  • Invalid self-membership, duplicate active membership, and use of an empty group are rejected with actionable errors.
  • Updating or deactivating a Party does not rewrite prior participation or decision history.
  • Unauthorized readers cannot retrieve protected Party details, and sensitive access is auditable.

docs.title: WIP
docs.text:

docs.title: Work In Progress (WIP) Process — PRD
docs.text: Status: draft for review. Owner: TBD. Date: 2026-11-02.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Work In Progress (WIP) process governs work after it is accepted and before it is finished. It makes each active item visible, gives it a clear owner and outcome, and helps work move through a small set of explicit states instead of accumulating unseen in queues or being treated as complete before it is ready.

WIP means work that has started but has not met its agreed completion criteria. The process is intended to make work flow and blockers visible; it does not prescribe a specific project-management tool, delivery method, or team cadence.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: When work is started without clear ownership, priority, or completion criteria, teams can take on more than they can finish. Partially completed tasks become difficult to track, blocked work can remain unnoticed, and stakeholders may mistake activity for progress.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Make accepted and active work visible in one agreed place.
  • Give each active item a named owner, clear outcome, and current status.
  • Limit starting new work when existing work is blocked or unfinished.
  • Make blockers, dependencies, and decisions visible so they can be addressed.
  • Define how work is reviewed and what qualifies as complete.
  • Use flow information to improve the process rather than judge individuals.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Mandating a particular tool, framework, meeting schedule, or estimation method.
  • Defining organization-wide priorities, staffing, or service-level commitments.
  • Treating the number of tasks completed as a measure of individual performance.
  • Setting numerical WIP limits before the team and its capacity are understood.

docs.title: Users and responsibilities
docs.text:
Role Responsibility Requester Describes the requested outcome and provides necessary context. Team or work coordinator Reviews incoming work, clarifies priority, and helps resolve capacity conflicts. Owner Moves an accepted item forward, updates its status, and raises blockers. Reviewer or approver Checks the result against the agreed completion criteria when review is required.

One person may perform more than one role. Every active item must have one clearly identified owner, even when several people contribute.

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
Requested → Ready → In Progress → Review → Done
                           ↘ Blocked ↗
  1. Request — Record the outcome needed, requester, context, and any known deadline or dependency.
  2. Triage — Decide whether to accept, defer, reject, or request clarification. Make priority and capacity trade-offs visible.
  3. Ready — Confirm the item is understood well enough to start: an owner is available, the expected outcome is clear, and required inputs are known.
  4. In Progress — The owner begins the work and keeps its status current. Before starting another item, the team checks its active WIP and agreed limits.
  5. Blocked — Record what is preventing progress, who can help, and the next action. The owner or coordinator follows up; blocked work remains visible and is not counted as complete.
  6. Review — Where review is needed, a reviewer checks the result against the completion criteria and either accepts it or returns it with specific follow-up work.
  7. Done — Close the item only when its agreed outcome and completion criteria are met. Record the result and notify relevant stakeholders.

docs.title: Work item requirements
docs.text:
An accepted item should identify:

  • The outcome or problem to address.
  • The requester and one accountable owner.
  • Its priority or relative order, as agreed by the team.
  • Completion criteria that make “done” observable.
  • Known dependencies, risks, and required review.

If an item is too large to complete or review as one unit, split it into smaller outcomes that can each be tracked and completed independently.

docs.title: WIP policy
docs.text:
WIP is the set of items that have started and are not yet done. The team should agree how it counts active work, including work in review and blocked work, before applying a limit.

When an agreed WIP limit is reached, the default response is to help finish, review, or unblock existing work before pulling in more. Exceptions should be explicit, with a reason and an owner for revisiting the decision. Numerical limits are intentionally left open until the team, work type, and capacity are known.

docs.title: Success measures
docs.text:
Establish a baseline before setting numerical targets:

Measure What it indicates Target Active items with an owner and completion criteria Whether WIP is sufficiently defined Agree after baseline Age of unfinished and blocked items Where work is waiting or stalled Agree after baseline Cycle time from start to done How long started work takes to complete Agree after baseline Work completed compared with work started Whether the team is finishing at a sustainable rate Improve from baseline Items reopened after being marked done Whether completion criteria and review are effective Agree after baseline

Use these measures to identify system bottlenecks and improve flow, not to rank individuals.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
The process is ready to adopt when:

  • The team agrees on its workflow states and what entry and exit mean for each.
  • A work item template captures the minimum information defined above.
  • The team agrees how to identify active WIP and how to handle a reached limit.
  • Blocked work has a visible reason, next action, and responsible person.
  • “Done” is based on agreed criteria rather than effort spent or status age.
  • Baselines and owners for reviewing flow measures are agreed.

docs.title: Assumptions and open questions
docs.text:
• WIP means Work In Progress in this document.
  • This is a general workflow proposal; the team, work type, existing tool, and current process have not been specified.
  • Which work types should use this process, and what work is exempt?
  • Who makes final priority and acceptance decisions?
  • Should review be required for every item or only specified work types?
  • How should urgent work enter without silently displacing committed work?
  • What WIP counting rules and limits fit the team's actual capacity?
  • What baseline period and targets should be used for the success measures?

docs.title: European Property Transaction WIP Process
docs.text: Status: draft; source specifications contain unresolved conflicts. Scope: process, lifecycle states, controls, and recorded country variations for fee-earning property transaction work. Entity, client, individual, and organization-specific details are intentionally omitted.

docs.title: What WIP means here
docs.text:
In this process, Work in Progress (WIP) is the financial record of authorized, fee-earning transaction work that has not yet been invoiced and collected. It is not a general task or staff-capacity tracker.

The process follows an authorized instruction from signing, through fee accrual and monthly reporting, to billing and payment or loss. The CRM deal stages describe transaction progress; the WIP record has its own finance lifecycle. They are related, but are not interchangeable.

docs.title: Process at a glance
docs.text:
Instruction authorized and signed
    → Create WIP record
    → Update fee, probability, expected completion, and reporting month
    → Reconcile at month end
    → Lock the reporting period on the 15th of the following month
    → Invoice issued: Billed
    → Payment received: Paid

Work abandoned or instruction withdrawn
    → Lost

Recurring fee arrangements may create a WIP line for each reporting period.

docs.title: Transaction progress and WIP status
docs.text:
The source material describes an eight-stage deal process, broadly progressing from origination and pitch through mandate, marketing, bidding, due diligence, exchange, and completion. A later architecture view maps deal-stage progress to a percentage used in WIP calculations. That mapping is not fully specified and is a future-state integration requirement; deal stage alone does not move a WIP record to Billed or Paid.

The stage names differ between source documents. One lists separate Pitch and Mandate stages and uses Exchange; another combines Pitch and Mandate earlier, calls a later stage Exclusivity, and labels the instruction stage differently. Reconcile the canonical stage list and the stage-to-percentage mapping before automating stage gates or accruals.

docs.title: WIP finance lifecycle
docs.text:
State Meaning and entry event Required information or rule Next states WIP Authorized work is tracked before invoicing. Create the WIP record only after the parent instruction exists and is active and signed. Reporting month is required and is stored as the first day of that month. Record fee values, probability from 0–100%, expected completion month, and applicable tax rate/currency. Billed or Lost Billed An invoice has been issued. Invoice number, invoice due date, and finance-system cross-reference are specified as required. Keep the invoice number once set. A probability below 30% at billing triggers a finance review alert; it does not, by itself, prohibit billing in the documented rule. Paid or Lost Paid Payment has been received in full. Record the date paid in full. Invoice number remains required. Terminal Lost Work is abandoned, the parent instruction is withdrawn/lost, or an invoice is cancelled after billing. No invoice fields are required for Lost. A parent loss/withdrawal is specified to cascade to related WIP lines. Terminal

The intended transitions are WIP → Billed → Paid, with Lost reachable from WIP or Billed. The source does not define a transition from Paid to Lost.

docs.title: Entry and creation rules
docs.text:
• The parent instruction must exist before its WIP record; the WIP record inherits its transaction classification, owning office, currency, and other reporting context.
  • WIP entry is described as requiring an active, signed instruction. The source labels this gate as inferred, not a fully confirmed rule.
  • Warn on a possible duplicate with the same parent instruction, expected completion month, and WIP status.
  • A recurring monthly or quarterly fee trigger may produce a separate WIP line for each period.

docs.title: Accrual and probability rules
docs.text:
• Review and update WIP monthly. The owner is expected to update probability and the current fee forecast.
  • Weighted office-retained pipeline is calculated as: office-retained fee × probability / 100.
  • Probability is editable while the record is WIP and is locked after it leaves WIP.
  • Capture the previous probability on change. If a record is billed from below 30%, flag it for finance review.
  • Warn about mixed or unexpected currencies. Do not sum unlike currencies as if they were one amount; reporting must account for currency conversion or separate currency totals.

docs.title: Billing and loss rules
docs.text:
• At Billed, require the invoice number, invoice due date, and finance-system reference as specified by the source.
  • At Paid, require the paid-in-full date and retain the invoice number.
  • A WIP record may be marked Lost when work is abandoned. Parent instruction loss or withdrawal is intended to mark its child WIP records Lost.
  • The source calls for finance review when a line is billed below 30% probability; it does not specify whether this review blocks the transition.

docs.title: Monthly controls and aging
docs.text:
Each WIP record belongs to a reporting month represented by the first day of that month. This replaces month-by-month spreadsheet tabs and allows historical periods to be reported consistently.

  • Month end: reconcile WIP and receivables and refresh aging reports.
  • Monthly: remind owners to review and update their WIP records.
  • Stale detection: a WIP line becomes stale when it remains in WIP after its expected completion month plus 30 days.
  • Weekly: alert the finance operations owner about stale lines, for re-forecasting or close-out.
  • Period lock: lock a reporting month on the 15th of the following month and record who locked it and when.
  • Enforcement: reject writes to fields covered by the lock, including writes through APIs or automated flows, not just edits through a user interface.

The precise set of locked fields, the authority and audit procedure for unlocking, and the handling of a stale record inside a locked period are not specified. These controls must be agreed before implementation. As written, a stale line may need its forecast or status updated after the reporting period has already locked.

docs.title: Recorded country differences
docs.text:
The supplied design material explicitly records these defaults:

Country of owning office VAT default Recorded distinction France 20% Initial market in the rollout sequence Spain 21% Added in a subsequent rollout phase United Kingdom 20% VAT default is listed; rollout timing is not specified

The VAT default follows the owning office, not the client's location. A cross-border client therefore does not, on its own, change the default rate. These are the defaults in the supplied design material, not confirmation of current statutory tax treatment; Finance and tax owners must validate applicable rates and exceptions before use.

Other recorded variations are operational rather than confirmed country-specific business rules:

  • Currency is inherited from the parent instruction. The source identifies at least EUR and GBP in the reporting environment and warns that mixed-currency totals need careful treatment.
  • Local finance-system routing is selected from the owning office. Country/office rollout and ledger integration differ, while consolidated finance integration is described as a later phase.
  • The documented rollout starts in France, then adds Spain and a further regional scope. The United Kingdom's rollout phase is not stated.
  • No additional country-specific lifecycle states, invoice requirements, aging thresholds, or transition rules were identified in the supplied notes.
  • Rules for countries beyond France, Spain, and the United Kingdom are not specified; do not infer them from these defaults.

docs.title: Open decisions and source conflicts
docs.text:
The source material is a draft and should not be treated as a final operating policy. Resolve these items with Finance, the process owner, and the relevant country teams:

  1. Canonical transaction stages: reconcile stage labels and ordering across the source materials; confirm whether transaction-stage progress drives any WIP calculation and define the mapping.
  2. WIP entry gate: confirm whether active status plus a signed date is mandatory before a WIP record can be created.
  3. Billing reference field: the newer core table definition does not include the finance-system reference on the WIP record, while the billing rules require it at Billed. Decide where it is stored.
  4. Period-lock field set: specify exactly which financial, status, and invoice fields become immutable and who may authorize an unlock.
  5. Stale/locked interaction: define how teams can re-forecast or close out stale records after their period locks.
  6. Parent-loss terminology: define which parent states trigger the Lost cascade and confirm consistent handling of withdrawal, completion, and abandonment.
  7. Low-probability billing: confirm whether a review alert is informational or a hard stop.
  8. Country and currency controls: validate VAT defaults, exceptions, currency conversion/reporting, local-system routing, and the United Kingdom rollout.
  9. Recurring fees and calculations: confirm how monthly or quarterly fee lines are generated and how gross fee and foreign-currency totals are derived.

docs.title: Source basis
docs.text: This summary is based on the supplied European WIP workflow, lifecycle, table, automation, finance-integration, period-locking, rollout, and open-question notes. It omits organization, entity, client, person, CRM schema, and system-instance details. Where the source says a requirement is inferred, contradictory, or unresolved, this document preserves that uncertainty rather than presenting it as agreed policy.

docs.title: European Property WIP Entity
docs.text: Status: draft, based on the newer shared finance-table definition. Related: euro property transaction wip process describes the lifecycle and operating rules.

docs.title: What the entity represents
docs.text:
A WIP record represents one fee-bearing unit of authorized property transaction work for one reporting period. It holds the financial forecast and, later, the invoice/payment facts for that unit of work.

It is a child of an instruction (the authorized engagement record), not a copy of the whole transaction or deal. One instruction can have many WIP records—for example, separate fee components, properties, or recurring reporting periods. The WIP record keeps selected instruction context alongside its own financial and lifecycle data so finance can report without reconstructing every relationship.

docs.title: Logical record shape
docs.text:
The following is a readable, organization-neutral view of a WIP record. It is not a literal API payload or finalized database schema.

wipRecord:
  identity:
    id: required
    reference: generated
    instructionId: required
    feeScheduleId: optional

  reportingContext:
    serviceLine: inherited
    transactionType: inherited
    sector: inherited
    clientAccountId: inherited
    entityAccountId: optional
    propertyId: optional
    leadNegotiatorId: inherited
    owningOfficeId: inherited
    currency: inherited

    grossFee: amount
    netFee: amount
    officeRetainedFee: amount
    probability: percentage
    weightedOfficeRetainedFee: calculated
    taxRate: percentage

  period:
    reportingMonth: required, first day of month
    expectedCompletionMonth: optional
    staleDate: calculated
    isStale: calculated

  lifecycle:
    status: required
    statusChangedAt: automatic
    previousProbability: automatic

  billing:
    invoiceNumber: required at Billed and Paid
    invoiceDueDate: required at Billed
    paidInFullDate: required at Paid
    financeSystemReference: required at Billed in the business rules

docs.title: Attribute groups
docs.text: Group What the record holds Identity and parent A unique record ID, generated human-readable reference, required parent instruction, and optional fee-schedule link. Reporting context Service line, transaction type, sector, client account, lead negotiator, owning office, currency, and optional property/entity references. Some values are copied from or inherited from the instruction to support reporting. Financials Gross fee, net fee, office-retained fee, probability, tax rate, and calculated weighted office-retained fee. The weighted value is office-retained fee × probability / 100. Period and aging Required reporting month (stored as the first day of the month), expected completion month, and calculated stale date/flag. The stale date is expected completion plus 30 days; a record is stale when it remains WIP after that date. Lifecycle One of WIP, Billed, Paid, or Lost, plus status-change time and previous-probability tracking. Billing Invoice number, due date, date paid in full, and finance-system cross-reference, conditionally required by status. Period control Period-lock flag, lock time, locking user, and comments. The exact locked field set and unlock authority remain undecided.

docs.title: Lifecycle on the entity
docs.text:
┌──────────────► Lost
                 │
WIP ─────────► Billed ─────────► Paid
  • WIP — fees are forecast and updated for the reporting period.
  • Billed — invoice has been issued; billing fields must be populated.
  • Paid — payment is received in full; payment date is recorded.
  • Lost — work is abandoned, the parent instruction is withdrawn, or an issued invoice is cancelled.

Paid and Lost are terminal in the documented lifecycle. The source does not define a transition from Paid to Lost.

docs.title: Important modeling rules
docs.text:
• The parent instruction is the WIP record's single service-line path. Service-line deals or engagements relate indirectly through the instruction; the current core design does not put separate service-line parent lookups on each WIP record.
  • Creating the WIP record depends on the instruction already existing, because some reporting context is inherited from it.
  • The instruction can have many WIP records. Separate reporting months or fee components should not be collapsed into one mutable lifetime record.
  • The reporting month is stored on each record, preserving period history rather than relying on separate monthly sheets.
  • Probability is editable while the record is WIP and is locked after it leaves WIP.
  • Inherited classification fields are denormalized snapshots for flat reporting. The source expects them to be populated from the parent when the WIP record is created.
  • A possible duplicate is identified by the same parent instruction, expected completion month, and status; the documented control is a warning.

docs.title: Known schema conflict
docs.text:
The newer shared-table definition is treated as authoritative here: the WIP record has one parent instruction and an optional fee-schedule reference. Older source material describes multiple service-line parent links, so it should not be mixed into this model.

There is a separate unresolved billing-field conflict: business rules require a finance-system reference at Billed, but the newer shared-table field list does not include that reference on the WIP record. The source places finance-system details on the parent instruction in one definition and on the WIP record in another. The owning system and exact field location need a decision before implementation.

The required-at-Billed rules for the invoice number and due date, and required-at-Paid rule for paid-in-full date, are stated in the source. This document does not resolve the missing finance-reference field.

docs.title: Country-dependent context
docs.text: The entity's operating process is common across the recorded countries. The source records owning-office defaults for VAT of France 20%, Spain 21%, and the United Kingdom 20%, and says the owning office—not the client's location—selects the default. Treat these as source-design values pending validation by Finance/tax owners, not as authoritative current tax advice. Other country-specific rules have not been established. See euro property transaction wip process for the country comparison and open decisions.

docs.title: Source basis
docs.text: This logical model is derived from the European WIP table specification, project overview, parent-instruction model, and open-questions notes. It abstracts the source's organization-specific table and field identifiers into business-neutral names. It is descriptive, not a replacement for an approved physical schema.

docs.title: Journey shapes
docs.text:
A journey is 1:1 with exactly one provider container. Which container depends on what was asked for:

Journey kind Provider container Endpoints Individual ID / AML / SoF / POA (+ monitoring) v2 transaction POST /v2/transactions, GET /v2/transactions/{id} Document verification v2 check (type: document) POST /v2/checks, POST /v2/checks/{c}/documents Know Your Business v2 check (type: company) POST /v2/checks, GET /v2/checks/{c} Title documents v3 check (type: title) POST /v3/checks, GET /v3/checks/{c}

Because provider containers are immutable in composition, the internal rule is:

One dispatch = one journey. Adding a requirement after dispatch means creating a new journey against the same matter and subject.

That is deliberate: it keeps the model honest about what Thirdfort allows (no additive tasks), and it makes later additional purchases (a SoF check a month after the ID check) explicit and separately auditable.

docs.text:
Requirement kind Thirdfort tasks Options we expose id_verification report:identity, report:footprint, report:peps method: nfc_preferred \| original \| lite, international_address_verification: bool, monitoring: bool aml_screening report:screening:lite (standalone) given_name, family_name, year_of_birth, country_iso3 address_verification report:footprint international_address_verification: bool proof_of_address documents:poa — proof_of_ownership documents:poo — source_of_funds report:bank-statement, report:bank-summary, report:sof-v1, documents:bank-statement party_role: purchaser \| giftor, bank_statements: automatic \| manual \| both company_check (KYB) company:summary, company:sanctions, plus optional jurisdiction-specific reports reports: [...], monitoring: bool title_documents title:plan-*, title:register-* title_numbers{freehold,leasehold} or address document_verification identity:lite via a document check document_type, front/back files ongoing_monitoring opts.monitored on report:peps / company:sanctions enable, later disable

Validation rules that belong in our layer, not the caller:

  • proof_of_ownership only valid for transferor/borrower/lessor roles.
  • aml_screening standalone requires DOB + last name + ISO3 country; the app-based products need only name + mobile.
  • Mobile number required whenever method includes an app journey; validate with libphonenumber and warn for the 23 unreliable-delivery country codes.
  • international_address_verification consent only meaningfully required for the listed non-UK countries.
  • Title documents: only order titles whose availability is IMMEDIATE, and only within HMLR hours.
  • Monitoring can never be enabled after creation if it was created disabled.

docs.title: Normalised outcomes
docs.text:
Two orthogonal fields, mirroring the provider but with clearer names:

  • requirement.state — requested, in_progress, completed, not_completed, cancelled. Derived from the provider report status where closed/complete ⇒ completed, and error/expired/rejected/unobtainable ⇒ not_completed.
  • requirement.outcome — clear, consider, fail, or null while incomplete.

Journey-level roll-up (see [[cdd-journey-state-model]] for the state machine) is ours alone: the provider never says "approved".

docs.title: Identity of the subject
docs.text:
• We are the system of record for subject PII. Thirdfort receives only what a check requires — name + mobile for app journeys, plus DOB/address for screening, plus document images for verification.
  • We should store the minimum and mark the rest as derived: after completion, the authoritative record is the provider report/PDF, which we copy into our own store (Artefact) so we are not permanently dependent on provider availability.
  • Retention is set by our own AML obligations (5 years from the end of the relationship) and not by Thirdfort's tenancy.

docs.title: What we deliberately do not model
docs.text:
• Thirdfort teams and stub users as first-class internal concepts. They are Binding.context_* values created and cached by the integration layer.
  • Thirdfort's print, ce, gid, uid metadata. Stored on the binding for support purposes, never surfaced in our API responses.
  • Provider versioning (v2/v3). It is a property of the binding, invisible to callers.

docs.title: Internal CDD process — PRD
docs.text:
What we are building, for whom, and what "done" means: one internal process for running customer due diligence across the firm, with Thirdfort as the verification provider behind it. This is the requirements counterpart to the design in [[internal-cdd-api]]; the API is the mechanism, the process is the product.

Status: draft for review. Owner: Solution Architecture. Date: 2026-10-15.

Related: [[internal-cdd-api]], cdd kyc domain model, [[cdd-journey-state-model]], thirdfort api notes, [[internal-cdd-api-openapi.yaml]], cdd poc app

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
CDD work today is arranged around a provider's verification toolkit: transactions, checks, tasks and reports. That shape does not match how the firm actually works a matter, and it puts the compliance decision nowhere at all — Thirdfort returns evidence and a result flag and stops.

We are building one internal process that owns the whole arc: plan what is required of a subject, dispatch it, chase it, watch it, assess the evidence, record the decision, keep the record, and keep watching afterwards. The provider becomes an implementation detail behind that process.

Concretely, this means an internal API and service layer in our own vocabulary — Matter, Subject, Journey, Requirement, Finding, Decision — that internal systems and advisers call instead of integrating Thirdfort directly. Which is the thing every team would otherwise rebuild, separately and worse.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Three distinct failures, one cause.

  1. The vocabulary is the provider's. Our systems think in matters, clients and files. Thirdfort thinks in transactions, checks and tasks. Every integration therefore begins with a translation layer, and each one translates differently.
  2. The truth is buried. Whether an ID check completed, which method actually completed, whether Source of Funds completed at all, and what is chargeable are all only recoverable by reading nested report payloads. An Enhanced NFC check can silently degrade to an Original ID. A transaction: closed means the PDF is ready, not that the client passed.
  3. Nobody owns the decision. The provider has no concept of a compliance decision, a reviewer, or an approval. So the decision — the point of the exercise — lives in spreadsheets, inboxes and individual memory, or is implicitly inferred from a provider status that does not mean what it appears to mean.

Add the reliability gap: Thirdfort documents no idempotency, no retry, no ordering guarantee, no rate-limit contract and no replay. Every team building directly inherits all of it.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• One process, one record. A matter's CDD is run and evidenced in one place, from plan to decision to retention, with an append-only audit trail.
  • The decision is explicit and owned. A named reviewer records an outcome, a risk rating and a rationale. Terminal states are earned, never inferred from a provider status.
  • Derived truth is delivered, not computed by callers. One summary call answers "where is this, what is outstanding, what evidence do we hold, what is chargeable".
  • The provider is replaceable, and invisible. Callers never name a transaction, a check, a task, a report, or an API version.
  • Failure is absorbed, not passed on. Duplicate dispatches, dropped webhooks, out-of-order events, provider outages and slow document generation are handled by the layer.

docs.title: Success measures
docs.text: Measure Target Journeys dispatched without an engineering ticket per new product all supported kinds Journeys with a recorded decision and reviewer 100% Reports-of-record held internally at end of relationship 100% Duplicate journeys created by a retried dispatch 0 Journeys stuck in a non-terminal state beyond threshold < 2%, and all explained on the timeline Chargeability derived from provider payloads by Finance 0

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• A provider-agnostic abstraction for its own sake. We abstract Thirdfort's model, not its features. A second provider is a repository rewrite behind the same domain, and that is enough.
  • Consumer-facing UI. The subject uses the Thirdfort app. We trigger and observe.
  • Exposing raw provider payloads or live provider URLs. No passthrough endpoints. The one escape hatch returns bytes we stored ourselves.
  • Replacing the firm's case management. We hold CDD, not the matter.
  • Being system of record for the subject's document custody beyond what regulation requires.

docs.title: Users and roles
docs.text: Role Needs Case handler / adviser Plan requirements for a subject, send it, see progress, chase, know what is blocking, hand off for decision. Compliance reviewer / MLRO The evidence in one place, findings in context, a decision to record, and an audit trail that survives scrutiny. The authority to approve, refer or reject. Ops / QC Find stuck journeys, resend invites, correct contact details, replay events, reconcile divergence between our state and the provider's. Origination / case systems Open a matter and request CDD without understanding verification. Machine-to-machine, idempotent, non-blocking. Risk & reporting Findings across the book, cycle times, chargeability. Finance Which requirements are chargeable, per matter, without re-deriving it from report payloads.

docs.title: The process
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P1["1<br/>Intake"] --> P2["2<br/>Plan"] --> P3["3<br/>Dispatch"] --> P4["4<br/>Engage"]
    P4 --> P5["5<br/>Observe"] --> P6["6<br/>Assess"] --> P7["7<br/>Decide"]
    P7 --> P8["8<br/>Retain<br/>and monitor"]
    P8 -. "new finding" .-> P6
# Phase Who Entry → Exit Failure modes the process must handle 1 Intake Case handler, origination Matter opened, subject captured → subject contactable and sufficiently described Duplicate subject records; missing mobile or DOB; unreliable-destination phone numbers 2 Plan Case handler Requirements chosen → plan validated against role and provider constraints Incompatible role/requirement pair; title unorderable or out of HMLR hours; a requirement added after dispatch 3 Dispatch Case handler, origination system Plan accepted → provider container created, invite issued Retried dispatch; provider outage; latency beyond budget 4 Engage Subject (Thirdfort app) Invite delivered → subject completes tasks Undelivered invite; wrong contact details; subject never starts; subject starts and abandons 5 Observe The layer Provider progresses → state and outcomes derived Duplicate, out-of-order or dropped events; slow v3 document generation; provider errors 6 Assess Compliance reviewer, ops Requirements terminal → evidence and findings understood Findings pending; report error/expired/unobtainable misread as a failed subject; a monitored hit arriving after the decision 7 Decide Compliance reviewer / MLRO Assessment done → decision recorded, journey closed Decision attempted against a cancelled or abandoned journey; a re-decision overwriting history 8 Retain & monitor The layer, compliance Journey closed → evidence retained, monitoring continues Artefacts unavailable from provider later; renewal silently lapsing; a post-decision hit with no route to reconsider

Journey-level states and the provider signals that drive them are in [[cdd-journey-state-model]]; the units involved are in cdd kyc domain model.

docs.title: Functional requirements
docs.text: Priority: Must (MVP cannot ship without it), Should (expected, deferrable once), Could (nice to have).

docs.title: Intake — the matter and the subject
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement SET-1 Must Every journey belongs to exactly one matter, and the matter reference travels upstream as the provider ref. SET-2 Must A subject is a person or a company, created once and reusable across journeys and matters. SET-3 Must A valid, contactable mobile number is required before any app-based requirement is planned; validate with libphonenumber and warn on the known unreliable-delivery country codes. SET-4 Must Date of birth, family name and ISO3 country are required before standalone screening. SET-5 Must Subject PII is stored encrypted on a minimum-necessary basis; reading it requires an explicit scope and every read is audited. SET-6 Should Subject records de-duplicate on name plus date of birth or company number, so a returning client does not become two people.

docs.title: Plan — what we are asking for
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement PLN-1 Must Callers express obligations in our vocabulary (requirement kinds). Provider task names and container types are never part of the caller's request. PLN-2 Must Role/requirement compatibility is validated before dispatch — for example proof of ownership is valid only for transferor, borrower and lessor roles. PLN-3 Must Requirements are fixed at dispatch. There is no endpoint to add one to a live journey; adding work means a new journey for the same matter and subject. PLN-4 Must Title requirements are orderable only when availability is IMMEDIATE and only inside HMLR hours (06:30–23:00 GMT, workdays). The constraint is surfaced before the attempt, not returned as an error from it. PLN-5 Should Before dispatch, the caller can preview what will be ordered and an indicative chargeability and count. PLN-6 Should A retried or duplicated dispatch intent cannot produce two journeys.

docs.title: Dispatch
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement DSP-1 Must One call dispatches a journey carrying one or more requirements, and returns a journey identifier and its initial state. DSP-2 Must Dispatch is idempotent under a caller-supplied key. Same key and same body returns the original response; same key and a different body is refused with 409. DSP-3 Must Provider container selection (v2 transaction, v2 check, v3 check) is internal. The caller neither sees nor chooses it. DSP-4 Must Provider unavailability never produces a partial journey. The dispatch either succeeds whole or does not happen. DSP-5 Should When provider dispatch exceeds the latency budget, the call returns 202 with a journey id rather than blocking the caller.

docs.title: Engage — getting the subject through it
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement ENG-1 Must Invite issuance is tracked as issued / delivered / undelivered, and is visible on the journey. ENG-2 Must An invite can be re-issued on demand. This is our capability; the provider has no resend endpoint. ENG-3 Should An undelivered invite raises an alert within the SLO window so ops can correct the contact details. ENG-4 Should Journeys expose time-in-state so ops can chase, and every chase attempt is recorded on the timeline.

docs.title: Observe — deriving the truth
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement OBS-1 Must Journey and requirement state is computed from a re-read of the provider resource, never from a webhook body. Duplicate events are no-ops; out-of-order events can only move state forwards. OBS-2 Must A reconciler re-reads every non-terminal journey on a decaying schedule, covering missed events. OBS-3 Must A polling-inbox fallback covers the case where our webhook endpoint is unavailable; messages are de-duplicated and acknowledged only after a successful reconcile. OBS-4 Must The identity method that actually completed is reported. An Enhanced NFC journey that degraded to an Original ID is Original, not Enhanced NFC. OBS-5 Must not_completed is never presented or reported as a failure of the subject. A skipped Source of Funds task is not-completed, not failed. OBS-6 Must One reviewer-facing summary states current state, per-requirement outcome, outstanding findings, blockers and chargeability, without the caller understanding any report payload. OBS-7 Must A provider 400 during v3 document generation is classified as upstream-not-ready and retried with backoff. It is never surfaced as a validation error.

docs.title: Findings — screening hits
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement FND-1 Must Screening hits (PEP, sanction, adverse media) are normalised into findings with a pending/dismissed state, independent of the provider's own hit model. FND-2 Must A finding can be dismissed or whitelisted with a reason, attributed to the actor who did it. FND-3 Must A change in the hit set on a monitored requirement raises new findings and requires an explicit re-decision. State never moves silently as a result.

docs.title: Decide
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement DEC-1 Must A human decision is recorded against the journey with an outcome, a risk rating, a rationale and a named reviewer. DEC-2 Must A journey reaches awaiting_decision only when every requirement has reached a terminal provider status. DEC-3 Must closed means a decision exists. It is never inferred from a provider status — a provider closed means the PDF is ready. DEC-4 Must A re-decision is a new immutable record that supersedes the previous one. Decision history is never rewritten. DEC-5 Must A decision against a cancelled or abandoned journey is refused. DEC-6 Should A decision cannot be recorded while findings are pending without an explicit acknowledgement, so the guard is visible rather than implicit.

docs.title: Monitor
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement MON-1 Must Monitoring is a flag on the journey, not a state. It can outlive closed, because a monitored check can produce a new report version months later. MON-2 Must Monitoring cannot be enabled after creation if it was created disabled. MON-3 Must Monitoring can be disabled on demand. Aborting a journey disables it automatically. MON-4 Must Monitoring renewal is warned at least 21 days ahead. MON-5 Must A post-decision hit raises a finding and a timeline event. It never silently moves a closed journey's state.

docs.title: Retain and audit
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement AUD-1 Must An append-only timeline records everything that happened, internal or provider-driven. Divergence between our state and the provider's is recorded, not smoothed over. AUD-2 Must The provider's authoritative artefacts (report JSON, results PDF, additional-documents ZIP, uploaded documents) are copied into our own store, so the report of record does not depend on continued provider availability. AUD-3 Must Provider bytes are served from our store. Callers never receive a live provider URL. AUD-4 Must Records are retained for the regulated period (currently 5 years from the end of the relationship) and anonymised rather than deleted by caller action. AUD-5 Must Evidence of consumer consent and of the firm's acceptance of provider terms is captured and filed with the matter. AUD-6 Must Cancellation is available at any non-terminal point. It is irreversible, and the process says so at the point of use.

docs.title: Bill and report
docs.text: ID Pri Requirement BIL-1 Must Chargeability is derived per requirement: ID per completed check, Source of Funds per property transaction grouped by identical ref, international address verification not chargeable where the address country is GBR. BIL-2 Must The provider ref format is canonical and stable, so chargeability grouping is deterministic. BIL-3 Should Chargeability is exposed on the requirement so Finance does not re-derive it from payloads. MI-1 Must Findings are queryable across journeys by status, category and date. MI-2 Should Cycle time and completion rate are reportable by requirement kind, to show where subjects stall. MI-3 Should Chargeability rolls up per matter and per organisation.

docs.title: Non-functional requirements
docs.text: Concern Requirement Dispatch latency p95 under 1.5 s including provider dispatch; otherwise queue and return 202 with a journey id. Read latency p95 under 300 ms from our store. No live provider call on a read path except an explicit refresh. Decision write Synchronous, durable and audited before it is acknowledged. Webhook receiver Acknowledges in under 100 ms; processing is asynchronous. Reconciliation Minutes while a journey is young, decaying to hours after 24 h. Environment isolation Sandbox and production are never mixed. A journey is pinned to one for its lifetime. Audit durability The timeline is append-only. No rewrite, no retro-edit, no backfill that hides history. Security OAuth2 client credentials, one client per system, scopes as the permission model. Encryption PII fields and artefacts encrypted at rest. Testability The contract is executable: a mock implementation of the API runs the whole process without a backend, as in cdd poc app.

docs.title: Compliance requirements
docs.text:
The process exists to satisfy CDD obligations, so these are requirements, not commentary. The specific regulatory citations below are assumptions to be confirmed with Compliance before build — they are recorded here so the confirmation is explicit rather than implied.

  • Customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence must be evidenced per subject before the relationship proceeds, and the evidence retained for the regulated period (currently 5 years from the end of the relationship).
  • PEP, sanctions and adverse media screening must be performed, and hits must be assessed and dispositions recorded with a reason.
  • Ongoing monitoring must continue for the appropriate period, and a post-decision hit must have a route back to a fresh assessment.
  • A named individual must own each decision, with the rationale recorded.
  • Source of funds must be evidenced for the relevant property transactions, and the evidence must survive independently of the provider.
  • Consent from the subject for their identity data to be processed must be captured.

Where regulation and the provider disagree — most visibly, where the provider says "closed" and the process still requires a human judgement — the process follows the regulation and the provider status is treated as an input, never an outcome.
