docs.title: Release phasing
docs.text: Phase Contents Exit 0 — POC The whole process simulated against a mock provider. Done — see cdd poc app. The vocabulary holds and the contract is executable. 1 — MVP Intake, plan, dispatch, observe, decide, retain. Identity and screening journeys (v2 transaction), artefacts, audit, decisions. One real journey per subject, decided and evidenced, with no engineering involvement per case. 2 — Depth Source of funds, proof of address and ownership, document verification, monitoring and findings, chargeability derivation, ops console. The common conveyancing journey runs end to end. 3 — Breadth KYB, title documents (v3), post-decision re-assessment, MI, subject reuse. The process covers the firm's matter types without exception handling by hand.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• The firm is a Thirdfort reseller, so chargeability derivation is required to bill. If that changes, BIL-1 to BIL-3 become reporting-only.
  • Thirdfort remains the sole provider for phase 1. The domain is designed so a second provider is a repository rewrite, not a domain change.
  • Provider tenant and stub-user mapping is established once per customer and cached.
  • 5 years from end of relationship remains the retention period. See Compliance above.
  • The subject's own experience happens in the Thirdfort app and is not ours to design. If that assumption breaks, ENG-1 to ENG-4 stop being sufficient.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Risk Impact Mitigation Provider key rotation is undocumented, and v3 documents no audience Blocks production auth One integrator per environment until answered; treat the token minter as a single point of failure and instrument it Upstream rate limits are undocumented Sandbox surprises, throttling in production Self-imposed global cap and queue; measure empirically before load Monitoring semantics across a closed journey are unresolved Post-decision hits could be mishandled Current design raises a finding and requires re-decision; never moves state silently Provider changes the report payload shape Derived truth silently wrong Reconcile from the resource, pin and test the derivation against fixtures, alert on unknown report types Title availability and HMLR hours constrain the process Journeys stall out of hours Surface the window pre-emptively rather than failing at dispatch

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Carried over from [[internal-cdd-api]], plus the ones this PRD exposes.

  • Monitoring across a decision. Re-open the journey, raise a new one, or add a finding and require an explicit re-decision? Current design is the third.
  • Multi-matter subjects. Reuse prior artefacts for a person verified on another matter, or force a fresh journey for evidential cleanliness? Leaning to a fresh journey referencing the prior one.
  • ref format. What is the canonical internal format, and is it stable enough to group chargeability by?
  • Rate limits and key rotation. Both undocumented upstream.
  • Who may decide. Is the decision scope limited to a compliance role, or does a senior case handler hold it for low-risk matters? This changes DEC-1 and the RBAC model.
  • EDD triggers. Which findings and risk ratings force enhanced due diligence, and is that expressed in the process or left to the reviewer's judgement?
  • Retention start point. "End of relationship" needs a precise definition and the process needs a field to hold it.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
The process is done when, for a real matter and subject:

  1. CDD is planned, dispatched and completed through the internal API alone, with no one touching Thirdfort directly.
  2. Every requirement's outcome, and the identity method actually completed, is correct without reading a provider payload.
  3. A not-completed requirement is reported as not-completed, and the reviewer sees why.
  4. A named reviewer records a decision with a rationale, and the journey is closed by that act and no other.
  5. An auditor can reconstruct the whole history — who asked for what, when, and on what evidence — from the timeline and stored artefacts, without provider access.
  6. Finance can derive what to charge without recomputing it from payloads.
  7. Killing our webhook endpoint mid-flight changes nothing about the eventual outcome.

docs.title: Thirdfort API notes
docs.text:
What the upstream Thirdfort API offers, reduced to the facts that matter for designing our own interface on top of it.

Source: https://thirdfort.stoplight.io/docs/api/b2edb775739e6-thirdfort-api (canonical: https://docs.thirdfort.com/docs/api). Content pulled 2026-10-15 from the Stoplight backing API (project cHJqOjM2MzI5, branch master; the tree lists 74 documentation nodes among 110 total nodes). See Appendix - refreshing these facts.

Related: [[internal-cdd-api]], cdd kyc domain model, [[cdd-journey-state-model]]

docs.title: Environments and versions
docs.text:
Base URL v2 sandbox https://sandbox.api.thirdfort.io/v2 v2 production https://api-v2.thirdfort.io/v2 v3 sandbox https://sandbox.api.thirdfort.io/v3 v3 production https://api-v2.thirdfort.io/v3
  • Two live versions with different scope. v3 only covers title documents (Checks, Documents, Titles). Everything else — transactions, checks (KYB/document), tenants, users, inboxes, events, companies — exists only in v2.
  • No deprecation or sunset notice for v2 anywhere in the docs. Assume both must be integrated and that our own API must not leak this split to callers.
  • Sandbox is functionally complete: real webhooks, real SMS (so don't use random phone numbers), mock verification data sources.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• Bearer JWT signed RS256 with our own 2048-bit RSA key. We keep the private half; Thirdfort gets the public half plus an email for the m2m account, and returns a kid.
  • Claims: aud, exp (= iat + 3600s), iat, iss, sub (both = m2m email). aud documented as https://sandbox.api.thirdfort.io/v2/ and https://api.thirdfort.io/v2/ — v2 only; no v3 audience is documented, and there is no documented mechanism for rotating the key. Both are open questions for Thirdfort.
  • Practical consequence: a token minter must exist, with jittered refresh well inside the 3600s window. This is the single point of failure for the whole integration.
  • Context headers are how resources get scoped. Mutually exclusive, team-id wins over tenant-id:
  • tenant-id — create under a partner tenant (access for everyone in it).
  • user-id — impersonate a stub user (attributes the request to a named individual).
  • team-id — direct-integration teams.

docs.title: Tenancy model
docs.text:
• Tenant = the business (law firm, agent) that bought Thirdfort. Its name is shown to the consumer in the SMS invite. Created with POST /v2/tenants ({name}); cannot be updated by API.
  • User = an individual at the company. For partner integrations we create stub users (type: "stub", roles ["app:web","transactions:user"]), which can only be impersonated, not logged into. POST /v2/users.
  • Consumer = the subject of the check, who uses the Thirdfort mobile app.
  • Partner integrations must map our customer → tenant and our user → stub user. Without it Thirdfort communicates with the consumer on behalf of us (the partner) instead of the tenant/user we represent — which is both a UX and an audit problem.
  • Commercial model matters to the design: reseller (we bill the firm) vs platform partner (Thirdfort bills the firm directly). Reseller requires us to derive which check actually completed in order to bill (see Billing and entitlement signals).

docs.title: Checks, transactions and tasks
docs.text:
Thirdfort's resource graph:

transaction (v2)          check (v2)              check (v3)
  request.tasks[]           request.reports[]       request.documents[]
  actor (consumer PII)      request.data{company}   request.data{address|title_numbers}
  → reports → PDF           → reports → PDF         → documents (PDF)
  • A transaction is the container for an ID/AML/Source of Funds journey for one consumer. type: "v2", required ref and request, name shown to the consumer, ref is ours.
  • A check covers document verification (type: "document") and Know-Your-Business (type: "company"); v3 uses type: "title".
  • Tasks are declared at creation and are not additive: you cannot bolt a new task onto an existing transaction. Adding a check later means a new transaction/check.
  • One or more tasks per transaction; status is per report, aggregated per resource.

docs.title: Task catalogue
docs.text:
Product Tasks Enhanced NFC ID report:identity (with opts.nfc: "preferred"), report:footprint, report:peps Original ID same three, without the nfc option Lite screening report:footprint, report:peps (no app involvement) Standalone screening report:screening:lite (needs DOB, last name, ISO3 country) Proof of address documents:poa Proof of ownership documents:poo (transferor, borrower, lessor only) Source of Funds report:bank-statement, report:bank-summary, report:sof-v1, optional documents:bank-statement Ongoing monitoring opts.monitored: true on report:peps (individuals) or company:sanctions (companies) International address verification opts.consent: true on report:footprint (needed only for a listed set of non-UK countries) Document verification POST /v2/checks with type: "document", report identity:lite, then POST /v2/checks/{check}/documents KYB company:summary + company:sanctions always; plus company:ubo, company:annual-accounts, company:annual-return, company:articles-association, company:beneficial-check, company:register-check, company:register-extract, company:register-report, company:shareholders by jurisdiction Title documents (v3) title:plan-freehold, title:register-freehold, title:plan-leasehold, title:register-leasehold

Giftor variation: request.actor.type: "giftor" switches the SoF questionnaire to the giftor flow.

docs.title: Statuses and enums
docs.text:
• Transaction status: open, closed, aborted (deleted also appears in the model enum).
  • Check status: open, closed (v3 adds deleted).
  • Report status: closed, complete, error, expired, rejected, unobtainable. Only closed/complete mean completed — everything else means "not done", not "failed the applicant".
  • Report result: clear, consider, fail. This is the compliance signal; it is separate from status.
  • Events: transaction, transaction:report, transaction:pdf, transaction:changes, transaction:share, check:report, check:pdf, check:changes, subscription:notification.
  • Per-task completion also surfaces as metadata.tasks.{type}.{status, completed_at}.

Two status traps worth encoding into our model:

  1. transaction: closed means the PDF is ready, not the client passed. A human decision is still ours to make.
  2. An Enhanced NFC check that fails chip read, liveness, or "no passport" silently degrades to an Original ID journey — the NFC breakdown comes back unobtainable. The identity report carries the evidence: breakdown.document non-empty ⇒ Original ID completed; absent ⇒ Enhanced NFC completed.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
Two supported mechanisms, configured per transaction/check at creation:

  • HTTP webhook — metadata.notify = {type: "http", data: {hmac_key, method, uri}}. Methods POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE (DELETE carries no payload). Payload envelope:

  { 
      "event": "transaction:report", 
      "timestamp": "...", 
      "type": "notify",
      "payload": { 
          "id": "...", 
          "resource": "reports", 
          "status": "closed",
          "uri": "/v2/transactions/{id}/reports/{id}", 
          "data": { 
              "type": "peps" 
          } 
      } 
  }
Signature: X-Signature header = HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body, keyed by the base64 hmac_key; verify constant-time before parsing. Keys are per-request, our choice. - Polling inbox — metadata.notify = {type: "inbox", data: {id}}; create with POST /v2/inboxes, read with GET /v2/inboxes/{id}/messages (unacknowledged by default, ?acknowledged=true for read, 204 when empty), acknowledge with PATCH /v2/inboxes/{inboxId}/messages/{msgId} body {"acknowledged": true} only.

Gaps that shape our design:

  • No documented retry policy, delivery guarantee, ordering guarantee, or replay. A webhook receiver must therefore treat delivery as at-most-once and reconcile by re-reading the resource.
  • No documented rate limits or 429 semantics.
  • Polling has no documented interval; messages must be de-duplicated by id.
  • Inbox acknowledgement is the only upstream read-receipt. We must acknowledge to avoid re-processing.

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text:
Need Call Transaction JSON (+ _embed=reports) GET /v2/transactions/{id}?_embed=reports Transaction PDF same, Accept: application/pdf (406 if negotiation fails) Extra uploaded documents same report URL, Accept: application/zip One report GET /v2/transactions/{t}/reports/{r} Normalised summary GET /v2/transactions/{id}/_summary KYB check JSON/PDF GET /v2/checks/{id} (Accept: application/pdf for the PDF) One KYB report GET /v2/checks/{c}/reports/{r}
  • _summary returns pii{address,dob,document,name} plus per-report {status, result, data} for address, document, facial_similarity, identity, peps, nfc. It is the cheapest single call for a normalised view — but its shape varies by check type.
  • Additional app-uploaded documents are not in the PDF; they arrive as a separate ZIP, signalled by report type documents:other (event transaction:report).

docs.title: Mutating operations
docs.text:
Action Upstream Abort a journey PATCH /v2/transactions/{t} {"status":"aborted"} — stops SMS, blocks further tasks, prevents PDF if not already generated, cannot be reopened, auto-disables monitoring Disable monitoring (individual) PATCH /v2/transactions/{t} {"changes":{"tasks":[{"type":"report:peps","opts":{"monitored":false}}]}} Disable monitoring (company) PATCH /v2/checks/{c} {"changes":{"reports":[{"type":"company:sanctions","opts":{"monitored":false}}]}} Whitelist screening hits POST /v2/transactions/{t}/reports/{r}/hits or POST /v2/checks/{c}/reports/{r}/hits, body {"dismissals":[{"id":"...","reason":"Irrelevant"}]} → 202 Share a report with a colleague POST /v2/transactions/{t}/events {"event":"transaction:share","payload":{"to":{"uid":"..."} \| {"email":"..."}}} Accept/reject a share PATCH /v2/events/{e} {"status":"accepted"\|"rejected"}; list via GET /v2/events Company lookup before KYB GET /v2/companies?jurisdiction=..&_q=name:X\|number:Y Title number search (v3) POST /v3/titles/_search; then GET /v3/titles/{title}/availability

Note the asymmetry: only status or changes per PATCH, and monitoring can be turned off but never on after creation if it was created off.

docs.title: Billing and entitlement signals
docs.text:
These matter if we bill, and they are all derived from report payloads:

  • ID checks are charged per completed check; SoF is charged per property transaction (grouped by identical ref). Use a consistent, prefixed ref — a matter/case/file reference.
  • Original ID vs Enhanced NFC (completed, not initiated): breakdown.document present on the identity report ⇒ Original ID.
  • SoF completed if any of bank:statement, bank:summary, sof:v1, documents:bank-statement is present with status: closed. Consumer skipping everything ⇒ no charge.
  • International address verification is not chargeable if footprint.breakdown.data.address.country == "GBR".

docs.title: Constraints and gotchas
docs.text:
• Title documents are HMLR-bound: 06:30–23:00 GMT on workdays only; out-of-hours checks close the next business day. Order only titles whose availability is IMMEDIATE; referred_to_documents are not downloadable.
  • v3 document generation is slow — sandbox returns HTTP 400 for roughly 3–4 minutes while a document is being generated. A 400 there is not a client error and must be retried with backoff.
  • Mobile number is mandatory for anything that uses the app; validated with libphonenumber. 23 country codes are flagged as unreliable for SMS delivery and warrant a UI warning.
  • Uploaded documents: PDF/JPEG/PNG only, 32 kb–10 mb, max 64 mpx; validated synchronously for blur, cut-off and document presence.
  • Ongoing monitoring runs 12 months and auto-renews; a subscription:notification arrives about a month before renewal and should prompt the user to continue or stop.
  • Error bodies come in two shapes: {"message": "..."} and a richer {message,name,code,status,error{reason,trace,type,details[]}}. Codes seen: 400, 401, 403, 404, 405, 406, 409, 422, 500, 503.

docs.title: Not present upstream
docs.text:
Confirmed absent from both specs and the guides — each absence is a gap our layer must fill:

  • Idempotency keys, ETags/optimistic concurrency, Retry-After, pagination on any collection, rate-limit headers, bulk/batch endpoints.
  • Any notion of a compliance decision, a reviewer, or an approval — Thirdfort returns evidence and results, never "accepted"/"rejected".
  • Any mapping to our matter/case identity beyond the free-text ref.
  • Re-issuing an invite (no resend SMS/invite endpoint).
  • Partial task addition to an existing transaction.
  • Deletion of a tenant or transaction.

docs.title: Inconsistencies found in the published specs
docs.text:
Worth knowing before we code against them:

  • v3 POST /checks path schema (request.documents[], flat data.address) disagrees with the prose guide and the unused CREATE_CHECK component (request.data.title_numbers|address, request.reports[], metadata.notify).
  • Check.request requires data and reports while v3 examples return documents[]; pdf examples use documents_id/type: title against a schema of document_id/type: check:pdf.
  • A CHECKS_LIST schema and a CREATE_CHECK requestBody exist in v3 but are not wired to any path — there is no v3 list endpoint.
  • GET /v3/documents/{document} is the only v3 operation with an explicit security block.
  • v2's PATCH /v2/events/{event} declares no 2xx response.
  • The docs link a Thirdfort Notion "API Hub" for UI/UX guidance; it was not read for these notes.

docs.title: Application project organisation
docs.text:
A standard shape for application projects: keep the knowledge vault (research, context, and exploration) separate from application repositories (code, infrastructure, and documentation that must evolve with the code). Each side points to the other; neither keeps a second copy of the other’s content.

This is the target structure for the vault’s /projects/<name>/ folders. [[cdd-poc-app]] is an example of the arrangement this replaces: application code living inside the vault.

docs.title: Why the current setup feels disorganised
docs.text:
Observed across the existing POC-* vaults:

  • One vault per project, duplicated boilerplate. Each vault carries its own AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, prompts/translate.md, and copilot/skills/ tree. Nothing is shared, so conventions drift.
  • Mixed concerns. POC-Thirdfort has app code (POC/lib/, tests, HTML wizards) alongside wiki notes. Code and knowledge have different lifecycles and tools; interleaving them makes both harder to manage.
  • Flat wiki folders don't scale. POC-Enterprise has 47+ files in one directory—SODs, vendor POCs, Entra ID configs, and architecture notes side by side.
  • Inconsistent shape per project. POC-Thirdfort has wiki/ + POC/, POC-NorthstarData has only wiki/, and POC-poc is an empty template. There is no consistent structure to return to.
  • The POC-poc template (/projects/<name>/ with a README per project) is the right starting point, but was never rolled out.

docs.title: Layer 1 — one knowledge vault
docs.text:
One vault for shared knowledge, with one folder per project and shared boilerplate at the root:

vault/
├── README.md
├── AGENTS.md
├── raw/
├── archive/
├── prompts/
└── projects/
    ├── thirdfort/
    │   ├── README.md
    │   ├── api-research.md
    │   ├── domain-exploration.md
    │   └── open-questions.md
    ├── enterprise/
    │   └── ...
    └── northstar-data/
        └── ...

Rules:

  • Use one folder per project; nest by topic once a project has roughly 10 notes.
  • Keep shared boilerplate (AGENTS.md, skills, prompts) at the vault root.
  • Make the project README the index: status, repo link, links to relevant research and repo-owned decisions, and last-updated date. Summarize context there, but link to ADRs rather than copying their decisions.

docs.title: Vault folders and workflow
docs.text:
The vault root README is a brief entry point. This document defines the structure and workflow; projects is the index linking to each project README.

  • /raw — capture inbox for notes, PDFs, screenshots, and links.
  • /wiki — organized notes and navigation pages, including the project index.
  • /projects/<name>/ — active project research and engagement notes.
  • /archive — processed raw material retained as a permanent record.
  • /prompts — shared prompts used by vault workflows.

For the capture-to-wiki workflow, add material to /raw, process it using translate, update the relevant wiki or project notes, then move processed material to /archive. Follow the vault rules in AGENTS.md: preserve raw and archived material, and read and merge an existing wiki entry rather than overwriting it. The vault is version-controlled so changes remain reviewable.

docs.title: Layer 2 — one application repo per deployable thing
docs.text:
Use the same basic shape for a throwaway POC and production; POCs simply have thinner content:

repo/
├── README.md
├── docs/
│   ├── design.md
│   ├── adr/
│   ├── prd.md
│   └── runbook.md
├── src/
├── tests/
├── infra/
├── config/
├── .github/workflows/
└── .gitignore

Conventions that matter most:

  • README is the contract: purpose, prerequisites, how to run it, and a link to the vault project folder. Aim for a fresh clone to run in under five minutes.
  • Docs-as-code: design docs, API contracts, runbooks, ratified PRDs, and ADRs live in the repo and are versioned with the code. The vault holds research and engagement context; the repo holds the current product requirements and build truth.
  • ADRs are lightweight records: one file per significant decision, such as docs/adr/0001-use-entra-id.md, covering context, options, choice, and consequences.
  • Keep infra/ separate from src/: this makes infrastructure-as-code reviewable and POCs easier to reproduce.
  • One repo per deployable thing: don't merge unrelated POCs into a monorepo or split one deployable POC across several repos.

docs.title: Writing repo documentation in Obsidian
docs.text:
Repo-owned documentation is still Markdown, so it can be written in Obsidian. Open the application repo folder as an Obsidian vault and edit its docs/ there; the files remain in the application repo and are versioned with the code. If using Obsidian settings or plugins in that repo, decide deliberately which shared configuration belongs in Git and keep machine-specific workspace state out.

The main knowledge vault and an application repo are separate Obsidian vaults. You can switch between them in Obsidian or open them in separate Obsidian windows. Obsidian does not combine independent folders into one vault view. If having all notes and repo documentation in a single Obsidian file tree is essential, this separate-vault arrangement may not fit; don't solve that by copying repo documentation into the knowledge vault, since that creates two sources of truth.

docs.title: Repo topology — where the code lives
docs.text:
The standard topology is N+1: one Git repo for the knowledge vault, plus one repo outside it for each deployable thing.

C:\Source\
├── Obsidian\Projects\<vault>\    ← vault Git repo
│   └── projects\<name>\          → pointer to repo
└── Repos\<app>\                  ← app Git repo
  • Not one repo for all projects. Unrelated POCs have independent lifecycles, CI, audiences, and clone histories. Partition repos by what ships together; partition vault folders by what you think about together. Those boundaries need not match.
  • Use a monorepo only when things genuinely ship together. For example, a CDD wizard and its API client belong together if they are tested and deployed as one. A separately deployed API is a separate repo.
  • Vault folder ↔ repo is not always 1:1: 1:1 is the norm; 1:0 for notes-only work (such as POC-Enterprise, where most SOD notes have no code); and 1:N when an engagement has several deployables.
  • Keep application code out of the vault. POC-Thirdfort-Vault\POC\ is the anti-pattern this structure replaces.

docs.title: The seam
docs.text:
Use one pointer each way; don't duplicate content:

  • Vault project README: Repo: <URL> | Status: <status and date>
  • Repo README: a link to the vault project folder, such as Knowledge notes: <vault project URL or agreed local link>

Archive a POC by marking its status in the vault README and making the repo read-only when appropriate. Do not move code into the vault.

docs.title: Documentation ownership
docs.text:
Each document has one home. Use this test: Would a change to the running product or its supported behavior require this document to change? If so, it belongs in repo/docs/. Does it change because research, engagement context, or understanding changed? If so, it belongs in the vault.

Content Home Architecture as built, API contract, runbook, ADRs, ratified PRD repo/docs/ Research, vendor facts, domain exploration, rejected discovery options, meeting notes vault/projects/<name>/ External artifacts (SODs, PDFs, screenshots) vault/archive/ Status, repo link, project index, links to repo decisions Vault project README

A domain model in the vault is exploratory; the implemented model or API contract belongs in the repo. Exploration may lead to a decision, which is recorded once as an ADR in the repo. The vault links to that ADR rather than restating the decision. The repo links back to the vault for engagement context.

One or two low-churn sentences describing the project may appear in both READMEs. Beyond that, link to the other source rather than copying it.

docs.title: PRDs
docs.text:
A PRD is normative: it says what should be built.

  • Draft: Keep it in vault/projects/<name>/, dated like other thinking notes, while it is being discussed and negotiated.
  • Ratified: Move it—not copy it—to repo/docs/prd.md. It is now the contract for the product. Map acceptance criteria to tests or another explicit verification method; changes to requirements should update the PRD.
  • Superseded: Keep prior versions in Git history. Record a deliberate scope change in an ADR; keep the discovery context in the vault and link to that ADR.

After ratification, the vault keeps discovery material and a PRD: <repo link> pointer, not an editable copy. If stakeholders edit the PRD outside Git (for example, in Word or SharePoint), treat the signed file as the artifact and archive it like an SOD; do not keep a competing working copy. Notes-only engagements with no repo keep their PRD in the vault.

For POCs, keep the PRD short: problem, success criteria, and non-goals. State how each criterion will be verified—by test, demo, inspection, or another suitable method—so the hypothesis can be meaningfully evaluated.

docs.title: Drift
docs.text:
Structure reduces drift but cannot eliminate it. The aim is one source of truth per fact and visible checks where the two layers meet:

  • Link rather than restate. Every copied fact is a potential drift site.
  • Review repo docs with behavior changes. When a code change affects documented behavior, the PR should update the relevant docs or explain why no update is needed. Use tests, contract checks, and CI to verify specific claims; a README or PR checklist alone does not guarantee documentation stays current.
  • Keep ADRs append-only. Supersede a decision with a new ADR (for example, 0002 supersedes 0001) rather than silently rewriting its history.
  • Date vault research. Notes are records of what was understood at a point in time, not current build truth. Include capture date, source, and open questions for facts that may change, such as vendor API behavior.
  • Show project freshness. Keep status and last-updated on the project README.
  • Archive deliberately. Mark the project archived in the vault and make the corresponding repo read-only when appropriate.

This structure cannot prevent an initially incorrect note, an unnoticed upstream change, or failures to follow review and CI practices. It makes ownership clearer and drift easier to detect; it does not replace those practices.

docs.title: Migration steps
docs.text:
1. Keep one shared vault and populate projects/<name>/ for each project. Retire duplicated per-vault boilerplate as projects are absorbed.
  2. Move application code out of vault POC/ folders into standalone repos. Keep code and build-truth docs together in each repo.
  3. Adopt docs/ + src/ + infra/ where appropriate, even for throwaway POCs, so they are reviewable and reproducible.
  4. For repo-owned Markdown, use Obsidian by opening the app repo as a vault. Keep vault research and repo documentation separate; link between them rather than copying.
